title: Too Hot for Lions: Tokyo Zoo Loses Three Lionesses in Record Heatwave
summary: Lions are supposed to be kings of the savanna, tough enough to handle blazing African sun. But at Tokyo's Tama Zoo, three lionesses — Mugi, Ichigo, and Luena — just died from something shocking: heatstroke. Yes, heatstroke. In Japan, temperatures have soared past 40°C (104°F), and the humidity makes it feel even worse. A zoo spokesperson said, 'Heat here comes with high humidity that is different from heat with dry air in Africa.' So even animals built for heat are in danger. The heatwave isn't just in Japan. South Korea hit a record 42.5°C (108.5°F) — the hottest in 122 years of weather records! The government declared a national disaster. At least 19 people have died, most of them elderly. Over 2,000 have gotten sick from the heat since May. In North Korea, state media showed packed water parks, but we don't know how many people are suffering there because the country doesn't share that information. What's causing this? Scientists say climate change, driven by burning fossil fuels, is making heatwaves more frequent and intense. The UN weather agency also warns that a strong El Niño — a natural warming of the Pacific Ocean — is starting this month, which could push global temperatures even higher. It's not just Asia: wildfires are raging in Greece, Spain, and France, and the U.S. is also baking. The lionesses' deaths are a sad reminder that extreme weather affects everyone — humans and animals alike. Zookeepers are now scrambling to add more cooling measures, but as the planet keeps heating up, even the mightiest creatures are at risk.
why_it_matters: If the planet keeps heating up, even strong animals like lions can get very sick, showing why taking care of the environment matters for all living things.

Article_Structure: WHO: Three lionesses named Mugi, Ichigo, and Luena who lived at Tokyo's Tama Zoo.
WHAT: They died from heatstroke during a record-breaking heatwave, with temperatures soaring past 40°C (104°F).
WHERE: In Tokyo, Japan, but the extreme heat also affected South Korea and other parts of East Asia.
WHY: Climate change is making heatwaves hotter and more intense, and the high humidity in Japan made it even harder for the lions to stay cool.

perspectives.description: They are worried and working quickly to add more fans, pools, and shaded areas to protect the remaining animals.
They warn that extreme weather events like this will keep getting worse unless the world reduces pollution from fossil fuels.
They declared a national disaster, showing just how serious the heatwave is and that many elderly people have been hurt.
